introduction-why-we-inject-failure.core: Distributed systems fail in ways nobody designed for: a dependency gets slow rather than down, a zone loses network, retries amplify load. Waiting for those failures to happen at 3 a.m. means learning under pressure. Chaos engineering deliberately injects controlled failures to find weaknesses, verify that resilience mechanisms actually work, and build team confidence before real incidents.

first_principles.problem: A failover mechanism that was 'tested' at design time fails during the first real regional outage.
truths: Untested resilience is assumed, not proven.
Complex systems have emergent failure modes.

analogy.title: Fire drills
analogy.story: You practise evacuating before a real fire to find blocked exits while it's safe.
analogy.breaks: Fire drills don't risk burning the building; chaos experiments must control blast radius.

example.title: First experiment
flow: Hypothesis: losing one cache node keeps p99 < 300 ms
Kill one Redis replica in staging
p99 jumps to 2 s: client didn't retry other replicas

check.q: What's the core purpose of chaos engineering?
check.a: To proactively discover weaknesses and verify resilience by injecting controlled failures, before real incidents expose them.

the-scientific-method-of-chaos.core: Chaos is experimentation, not random breakage. Define steady state as a measurable normal (SLIs); hypothesise that it holds under a specific fault; introduce the fault realistically in a controlled scope; compare against a control group or baseline; and accept or refute the hypothesis. Start small (staging, one instance), automate abort conditions, and expand scope as confidence grows, eventually running in production.

first_principles.problem: An engineer randomly kills pods 'to see what happens' and causes an outage without learning anything specific.

analogy.title: A clinical trial
analogy.story: A clear hypothesis, controlled dosage, a control group, monitoring, and stopping rules if harm appears.
analogy.breaks: Trials take months; chaos experiments take minutes but still need rigour.

code.text:
name: payments-db-failover
steady_state: checkout success ≥ 99.5%, p99 < 800 ms
hypothesis: promoting replica keeps success ≥ 99% with < 30 s disruption
fault: force RDS failover (primary reboot with failover)
scope: prod, 10:00–11:00 Tue, on-call present
abort: success < 98% for 2 min OR p99 > 3 s
result: TBD

check.q: What's the difference between chaos engineering and randomly breaking things?
check.a: Chaos engineering uses explicit hypotheses, measured steady state, controlled scope and abort conditions to learn something specific.

step-1-the-steady-state-hypothesis.core: Steady state is the system's normal, observable behaviour, ideally user-facing business and SLI metrics (orders per minute, success rate, p99) rather than CPU. The hypothesis states that this steady state will continue despite a specific fault: 'If one AZ loses network, checkout success stays ≥ 99% and p99 < 1 s.' Without a measurable steady state you can't tell whether an experiment succeeded or harmed users.

first_principles.problem: A chaos test is declared 'fine' because pods restarted, while checkout errors quietly doubled.

analogy.title: A doctor's baseline vitals before a stress test
analogy.story: You need normal heart rate and blood pressure to judge whether the treadmill test revealed a problem.
analogy.breaks: Vitals vary per patient; steady state also varies by time of day.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Experiment verified against a user-facing SLI.

check.q: Why should steady state use user-facing metrics rather than infrastructure metrics?
check.a: Infrastructure can look fine while users suffer; user-facing SLIs show the real impact of the fault.

step-2-fault-injection-the-attacks.core: Inject faults that resemble real failures. Resource faults: CPU, memory and disk exhaustion. State faults: kill processes, pods, nodes or a whole AZ. Network faults: latency, loss, partitions, DNS failure, blackholed dependencies. Application faults: errors or delays in specific calls (service mesh fault injection). Time faults: clock skew. Latency faults are often more revealing than outright failures, because slow is harder to handle than down.

first_principles.problem: A team only ever tests pod kills, which Kubernetes handles easily, and misses that a slow dependency exhausts thread pools.

analogy.title: A flight simulator's failure menu
analogy.story: Pilots train for engine loss, but also instrument failure, bad weather and slow responses.
analogy.breaks: Simulators are fully isolated; production chaos affects real users if uncontrolled.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Reveals whether checkout times out gracefully when fraud is slow.

code.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: { name: fraud-chaos }
spec:
  hosts: [fraud]
  http:
    - match: [{ headers: { x-chaos: { exact: "on" } } }]
      fault: { delay: { percentage: { value: 50 }, fixedDelay: 3s } }
      route: [{ destination: { host: fraud } }]
    - route: [{ destination: { host: fraud } }]

check.q: Why is injecting latency often more valuable than killing services?
check.a: Slow dependencies tie up threads and connections and trigger retries, causing cascading failures that clean crashes don't.

tools-of-the-trade.core: Chaos tools range from Kubernetes-native platforms (Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos) with CRDs for pod, network, IO and time faults, through managed cloud services (AWS Fault Injection Service, Azure Chaos Studio) that inject at cloud-API level such as stopping instances, failing AZ networking or throttling APIs, to commercial platforms (Gremlin) and code-level frameworks (Toxiproxy, Chaos Toolkit). Good tools offer scoping, scheduling, abort conditions and audit logs.

first_principles.problem: A team writes ad-hoc scripts to kill pods, with no safety controls or record of what was run.
derivation: **AWS FIS / Azure Chaos Studio** for cloud.

analogy.title: A professional stunt team vs amateurs
analogy.story: Pros use rigs, safety lines and rehearsed plans; amateurs just jump.
analogy.breaks: Stunts are one-off; chaos should be continuous.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 30% of payments pods get 400 ms latency for 5 minutes.

check.q: What safety feature should every chaos tool used in production support?
check.a: Stop/abort conditions tied to health metrics or alarms that automatically halt the experiment.

gamedays-learning-together.core: A GameDay is a scheduled, facilitated exercise where teams run chaos scenarios together, such as a region failure, dependency outage or data corruption. They practise detection, response, communication and runbooks in real time, then hold a blameless review. GameDays test people and processes as much as systems: did alerts fire, did the right people get paged, did runbooks work, did status updates go out?

first_principles.problem: The team's disaster recovery runbook was written two years ago and nobody has ever followed it.
truths: Practice under low stakes builds skill.

analogy.title: A fire brigade training exercise
analogy.story: Crews practise together with real equipment so the real call goes smoothly.
analogy.breaks: Fire drills are routine; GameDays need fresh scenarios to stay useful.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Concrete fixes before a real outage.

check.q: Besides system resilience, what do GameDays test?
check.a: Detection, alerting, paging, runbooks, decision-making and communication: the human and process side of incidents.
